items.title: Recommended Study Strategy
items.text:
1. Follow the Topic Order: Topics are arranged progressively; subsequent concepts build on earlier foundations.
  2. Hand-Trace Every Example: Don't just read tables and Gantt charts—draw them out on scratch paper.
  3. Verify with Code: Run the small lab code snippets provided in each topic to inspect actual OS behavior.
  4. Drill the MCQ Patterns: Review the "Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns" section in each topic to avoid tricky traps.
  5. Simulate Timed Practice: Complete the end-of-topic practice problems before checking the collapsed answers.

items.title: Topic 01: Introduction & Architecture
items.text: Source: Lecture 1.1–1.3 (Unit 1) + Textbook Ch. 1–2 ({TEXTBOOKS})

items.title: Hardware Privilege Modes
items.text:
Modern processors implement hardware-enforced protection boundaries (rings) to isolate user applications from privileged kernel instructions.

[ User Applications (Ring 3: Unprivileged) ]
                  │
          System Call Trap
                  ▼
[ Kernel Subsystems (Ring 0: Privileged / Supervisor) ]
                  │
                  ▼
[ Physical CPU, Registers, Memory & I/O Controllers ]

items.title: Core Architecture Concepts
items.text:
• Dual-Mode Operation:
  • User Mode (Ring 3): Execution restricted; privileged CPU instructions forbidden.
  • Kernel / Supervisor Mode (Ring 0): Full hardware access; memory management and device control enabled.

  • Mode Bit: Hardware register bit indicating current execution level (e.g., 0 for kernel, 1 for user).

  • Mode Transition Triggers:

  • Software Interrupt / System Call (syscall, sysenter, int 0x80): User process requests an OS service.
  • Hardware Interrupt: External peripheral device signals an event (keyboard press, timer tick, network packet).
  • Hardware Trap / Fault: CPU-detected synchronous exception (division by zero, page fault).

items.title: 01.2 System Calls vs. Library Calls
items.text: Property Standard Library Call (e.g., printf) System Call (e.g., write) Execution Ring User space (Ring 3) Kernel space (Ring 0) Context Switch No privilege change Enforces mode switch via interrupt/trap Buffering User-space stream buffer (FILE *) Kernel page cache & device buffers Performance Cost Low overhead function call High overhead (saves registers, switches stack)

items.title: 01.3 Standard Lab Implementation Example
items.text:
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>

int main(void) {
    const char *msg = "Executing direct write() syscall\n";
    // Directly invokes Ring 0 write syscall without userland buffering
    write(STDOUT_FILENO, msg, strlen(msg));
    return 0;
}

items.title: 01.4 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Privilege Separation: Dual-mode hardware is essential for protecting the OS from errant or malicious user code.
  2. Transition Path: All transitions from User Mode to Kernel Mode occur strictly via traps, syscalls, or hardware interrupts.
  3. Overhead Consideration: System calls require state preservation and context switching, making batching and buffering crucial for performance.

items.title: 01.5 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
MCQ Pattern: Mode Bit Transitions

When an external timer interrupt occurs during the execution of a user-level process:

  • A) The mode bit stays set to user mode until the scheduler runs.
  • B) The hardware switches the mode bit to kernel mode before invoking the interrupt handler.
  • C) The user process terminates immediately.
  • D) The interrupt handler executes in user mode with elevated priority.
Explanation

Hardware interrupts force the processor into kernel mode (Ring 0) automatically so that the kernel's Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) can run safely.

items.title: Topic 02: Process Concepts & Lifecycle
items.text: Source: Lecture 1.4–1.6 (Unit 1) + Textbook Ch. 3 ({TEXTBOOKS})

items.title: 02.1 Process State Model
items.text:
A process transitions through discrete execution states managed by the OS scheduler:

[ New ] ──Admit──► [ Ready ] ◄──Interrupt── [ Running ] ──Exit──► [ Terminated ]
                       ▲                         │
                       │                         ▼
                       └─── I/O Event Done ─── [ Waiting / Blocked ]

items.title: Process Control Block (PCB) Contents
items.text:
• Process ID (PID): Unique integer identifier.
  • Process State: Running, Ready, Waiting, etc.
  • Program Counter (PC): Memory address of next instruction.
  • CPU Registers: General-purpose registers, stack pointer, flags.
  • Memory Management Info: Base/limit registers, page table pointers.
  • Accounting & Scheduling: Priority, CPU execution time limits.
  • I/O Status: Open file descriptors, allocated devices.

items.title: 02.2 Process Creation & Destruction in Unix
items.text:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

int main(void) {
    pid_t pid = fork();

    if (pid < 0) {
        perror("Fork failed");
        return 1;
    } else if (pid == 0) {
        // Child Process
        printf("Child process running with PID: %d\n", getpid());
        _exit(0);
    } else {
        // Parent Process
        wait(NULL); // Reap child to avoid zombie state
        printf("Parent reaped child.\n");
    }
    return 0;
}

items.title: 02.3 Zombie vs. Orphan Processes
items.text: Type Condition Resolution Zombie Process Child has terminated, but parent has not called wait() Parent calls wait(), or if parent dies, init/systemd reaps it. Orphan Process Parent terminated while child continues running Re-parented to init (PID 1) / systemd, which periodically calls wait().

items.title: 02.4 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. PCB as Identity: The PCB is the single source of truth for process tracking in kernel memory.
  2. Context Switching Cost: Involves saving register states, flushing pipeline caches, and loading memory tables.
  3. Reaping Requirement: Every terminated child process must be collected by its parent to release its PCB slot.

items.title: Topic 03: Synchronization & IPC
items.text: Source: Lecture 2.1–2.4 (Unit 2) + Textbook Ch. 5–7 ({TEXTBOOKS})

items.title: 03.1 Race Conditions & The Critical Section Problem
items.text: A race condition occurs when multiple concurrent processes or threads access and manipulate shared data, and the final outcome depends on the non-deterministic order of instruction execution.

items.title: The Three Critical Section Requirements
items.text:
1. Mutual Exclusion: If process $P_i$ is executing in its critical section, no other processes can be executing in their critical sections.
  2. Progress: If no process is executing in its critical section and some processes wish to enter, only those processes not executing in their remainder sections can participate in deciding who enters next.
  3. Bounded Waiting: There exists a bound on the number of times that other processes are allowed to enter their critical sections after a process has made a request to enter and before that request is granted.

items.title: 03.2 Semaphores vs. Mutexes
items.text: Feature Mutex Counting Semaphore Ownership Locked by and unlocked exclusively by the owning thread No ownership; any thread can signal/post Value Range Binary (0 or 1) Non-negative integer (0 to $N$) Typical Use Strict mutual exclusion for a single critical section Resource pooling & cross-thread signaling

items.title: 03.3 POSIX Synchronization Primitives in C
items.text:
#include <pthread.h>
#include <semaphore.h>
#include <stdio.h>

pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
sem_t sem_items;

void *worker(void *arg) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
    // Protected Critical Section
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
    return NULL;
}

items.title: 03.4 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Mutual Exclusion: Non-negotiable requirement to eliminate race conditions on shared memory.
  2. Deadlock Danger: Careless lock acquisition ordering produces cyclic wait deadlocks.
  3. Hardware Support: Atomic instructions (test_and_set, compare_and_swap) form the bedrock of user-level locking primitives.

items.title: Topic 15: Main Memory — Hardware, Address Translation, Dynamic Loading/Linking, mmap
items.text: Source: Lecture 3.1 (Unit 3) + Textbook Ch. 8 (Silberschatz Ch. 8, Stallings Ch. 7)

items.title: Logical vs Physical Address
items.text:
Logical Address (CPU) → MMU → Physical Address (Memory)
  • Logical (Virtual) Address: Generated by CPU during execution; seen by programmer and user process.
  • Physical Address: Loaded into memory address register (MAR) of physical RAM.
  • MMU (Memory Management Unit): Hardware device mapping virtual to physical addresses at runtime.

items.title: Hardware Support
items.text:
• Base / Limit Registers: Provide basic hardware relocation and memory protection.
  • Base Register: Holds the smallest physical memory address allocated to the process.
  • Limit Register: Specifies the range (size) of the logical address space.
  • Legal Range Condition: 
    0 ≤ Logical Address < Limit
  • Address Computation: 
    Physical Address = Base + Logical Address
  • Trap Mechanism: If Logical Address ≥ Limit, the CPU hardware triggers an addressing trap (Segmentation Fault / Illegal Memory Access) to the OS kernel.
  • Memory Management Unit (MMU): Performs run-time address translation transparently to software.
  • Page Table Base Register (PTBR): Processor control register pointing to the base of the current process's active page table.

items.title: Memory Allocation Strategies
items.text:
When allocating contiguous variable-sized memory blocks from a pool of free holes:

Strategy Description Characteristics & Trade-offs First Fit Allocate the first hole that is large enough Fastest search; stops at the earliest available candidate. Best Fit Allocate the smallest hole that is large enough Requires scanning the entire list (unless ordered); leaves small unusable leftover holes. Worst Fit Allocate the largest available hole Leaves the largest remaining hole (more usable for subsequent allocations); slowest in practice.

items.title: Memory Protection
items.text:
• Valid / Invalid Bits: Hardware flags in translation tables indicating whether an address falls within the process's allocated address space.
  • Protection Bits: Specify access permissions (Read, Write, Execute) per page or segment.
  • System Traps: Any unauthorized write to a read-only page triggers a hardware protection violation.

items.title: Shared Pages
items.text:
• Read-Only Code Sharing: Pure code (reentrant routines, shared C libraries) mapped with identical physical addresses across multiple process address spaces.
  • Copy-On-Write (COW): Pages shared read-only upon process creation (fork()); physical copy allocated only when either process writes to the page.

items.title: Dynamic Loading
items.text:
• Routines are kept on secondary storage in relocatable load format.
  • A routine is loaded into memory only when called by the running program.
  • Unused routines (e.g., error handling code, diagnostic routines) are never loaded into physical RAM.
  • Benefit: Significantly reduces working memory footprint and accelerates application boot time.

items.title: Dynamic Linking
items.text:
• Resolving external symbols and linking is postponed until program execution time.
  • A small stub replaces library routine calls to locate and load the shared object if not already resident.
  • Single Shared Copy: Only one copy of the library code resides in physical RAM across all processes.
  • Shared Library Extensions: .so (Linux Shared Objects), .dll (Windows Dynamic Link Libraries), .dylib (macOS).

items.title: 15.4 Memory-Mapped Files (mmap())
items.text:
The mmap() system call maps a file or anonymous memory region directly into the process's virtual address space, converting disk I/O operations into standard pointer memory reads and writes.

#include <sys/mman.h>

void *mmap(void *addr, size_t len, int prot, int flags, int fd, off_t offset);
// Maps file descriptor fd into memory — treats file I/O as memory access

int munmap(void *addr, size_t len);  // Unmaps the designated memory region

items.title: Parameters & Configuration Flags
items.text: Parameter Type / Macro Description addr void * Starting address hint (NULL requests the kernel to select a page-aligned address) len size_t Length in bytes of the memory mapping prot Bitwise OR Page access protections: PROT_READ, PROT_WRITE, PROT_EXEC, PROT_NONE flags Bitwise OR MAP_SHARED (updates flush to disk & visible to other processes) vs. MAP_PRIVATE (COW mapping; changes remain private) fd int Open file descriptor from open() syscall offset off_t Offset within the file to begin mapping (must be an integer multiple of page size)

items.title: Common Systems Use Cases
items.text:
1. High-Throughput File I/O: Eliminates repetitive read() / write() syscall overhead and redundant buffer copying.
  2. Shared Memory IPC: Combining MAP_SHARED with MAP_ANONYMOUS creates shared memory regions between parent and child processes.
  3. Executable & Shared Library Loading: Operating system dynamic linkers (ld.so) use mmap to load text and data segments.
  4. Out-of-Core Processing: Managing database indexes and video files larger than physical RAM via automatic demand paging.

items.title: 15.5 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Base & Limit Registers: Provide fundamental hardware protection and dynamic relocation.
  2. MMU Function: Seamlessly translates CPU-issued logical addresses to MAR physical memory locations.
  3. Contiguous Allocation: First Fit offers optimal speed; Best Fit minimizes leftover hole size but worsens external fragmentation.
  4. Dynamic Loading vs. Linking: Loading defers routine allocation until called; linking defers external symbol resolution and enables RAM sharing.
  5. Memory Mapping (mmap): Bridges memory management and disk storage by treating file blocks as virtual memory addresses.

items.title: 15.6 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
MCQ Pattern 1: Base and Limit Register Traps

A CPU generates a logical address of 0x0350. The base register contains 0x4000 and the limit register contains 0x0300. Which action occurs?

  • A) The physical address 0x4350 is accessed.
  • B) A trap (segmentation/addressing error) is generated by the hardware.
  • C) The address wraps around to 0x4050.
  • D) The limit register is dynamically expanded.
Explanation

The legal address condition is 0 <= Logical Address < Limit. Here, 0x0350 >= 0x0300, which violates the limit boundary. The MMU hardware intercepts this and generates a trap.

MCQ Pattern 2: MAP_SHARED vs. MAP_PRIVATE Semantics

When process $P_1$ writes to a memory region mapped with mmap() using MAP_PRIVATE, which statement is true?

  • A) The underlying disk file is immediately updated.
  • B) Other processes mapping the same file see the change.
  • C) A private copy-on-write page is created for $P_1$, leaving the original file unchanged.
  • D) The kernel terminates $P_1$ with SIGSEGV.
Explanation

MAP_PRIVATE configures copy-on-write (COW) semantics. Any modifications are isolated to the calling process and are not committed to the underlying file.

items.title: Problem 1: Base/Limit Address Validation
items.text:
Given: - Base Register = 21000 - Limit Register = 4500

Evaluate whether the following logical addresses are legal and determine their resulting physical addresses: 1. Logical Address 250 2. Logical Address 4500 3. Logical Address 3800

Solution Trace
  1. 250 < 4500 → Legal. Physical Address = 21000 + 250 = 21250.
  2. 4500 >= 4500 → Illegal. Triggers hardware trap (limit violation).
  3. 3800 < 4500 → Legal. Physical Address = 21000 + 3800 = 24800.

items.title: Problem 2: Dynamic Allocation Strategy Trace
items.text:
Given free holes in memory of sizes: 100 KB, 500 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB, and 600 KB (in order). Trace which hole is selected for an incoming request of 212 KB under: 1. First Fit 2. Best Fit 3. Worst Fit

Solution Trace
  • First Fit: Scans in order → 100 KB (too small) → 500 KB hole chosen (leaves 288 KB hole).
  • Best Fit: Scans all holes → candidate holes ≥ 212 KB are 500 KB, 300 KB, 600 KB. Smallest candidate is 300 KB hole chosen (leaves 88 KB hole).
  • Worst Fit: Scans all holes → largest hole is 600 KB hole chosen (leaves 388 KB hole).
